analysis.one_liner: Requires every decennial census questionnaire to ask whether the respondent is a U.S. citizen.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing or a vote: introduced in May 2019, it was sent to the Homeland Security Committee and died there with zero cosponsors when the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have required the 2020 census and all future censuses to include a checkbox asking each person whether they are a U.S. citizen or national. Census experts and courts warned during this period that adding a citizenship question depresses responses from immigrant and mixed-status households, making the population count less accurate. The bill was referred to the Senate Homeland Security Committee on the day it was introduced and never moved again.
analysis.who_benefits: If it had passed, the main beneficiaries would be political interests that would gain relative representation when census counts understate immigrant-heavy communities — the census drives House seats, Electoral College votes, and state legislative districting. Communities and states with large immigrant populations would bear the cost through undercounts that shrink their share of representation and federal funding.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Political interests gaining from altered census counts

how_it_helps.text: The bill would have required every decennial census questionnaire to include a checkbox asking whether the respondent is a citizen or national of the United States, starting with the 2020 census and each census thereafter [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: Immigrant and mixed-status households, and the communities they live in, would bear the cost: a citizenship question historically lowers census participation among those households, and an undercount costs them representation and federal program dollars.

drawbacks.text: A citizenship question reduces participation among immigrant and mixed-status households, which makes the overall population count less accurate and distorts the data used to apportion House seats and draw districts [S2].

The bill also carries an operational cost: it would lock a question into the census statute that the Census Bureau had long treated as best asked on a separate survey, not the count used for apportionment [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The stated aim — a separate count of citizens — was already achievable through the Census Bureau's other surveys; the bill's actual effect would have been to place a citizenship checkbox on the apportionment count itself, with the accuracy cost falling on immigrant communities and, downstream, on everyone who relies on accurate census data. The benefit to the public was small; the cost was real.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent straight to the Senate Homeland Security Committee, which never acted on it, and it expired when the 116th Congress ended with no cosponsors and no vote.

narrative.text: Sen. Steve Daines introduced the bill on May 8, 2019, and it was read twice and referred to the Committee on Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs the same day [S1][S5].
The bill had no cosponsors at any point [S4].
No further action was taken after the referral; the bill never received a hearing, a committee vote, or a floor vote, and it died at the end of the 116th Congress on January 3, 2021 [S5].
The 2020 census was conducted without a citizenship question, after the Supreme Court blocked the Commerce Department's attempt to add one in 2019.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Communities vulnerable to a census undercount are better off, since the 2020 count went forward without the citizenship question the bill would have mandated. No legislator or industry gained anything from the bill's death, because it had built no support to lose.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Communities vulnerable to a census undercount

for.name: Sen. Steve Daines
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and it was referred to committee on his sponsorship.

for.name: President Donald Trump
for.what_they_did: His administration sought to add a citizenship question to the 2020 census during this period, the broader effort this bill aligned with.

sides.party_line_note: No votes or hearings occurred, so the partisan shape never got tested; the bill drew no cosponsors of either party and died in committee.

industries.note: A citizenship question would depress responses in immigrant-heavy areas, shifting the population counts that determine House seats, Electoral College votes, and district lines toward areas with fewer noncitizens. Any gain for those political interests came directly out of the accuracy of the count that ordinary people rely on.
